ENGINEERING NOTES / 19 OCTOBER 2026

What if a sheet
could be a screen?

One shared frame format. A browser studio. Real spreadsheet cells. Here is the reasoning behind the system, and where its limits are.

The pipeline we built

Video / webcam → Resize + quantize → Indexed frames → Browser / ODS / Calc

The browser decodes local videos and samples the webcam using standard media APIs. Each tiny sampled frame becomes a row-major array of palette indices. The same data drives the preview, the exported LibreOffice document, and the native Calc companion. For formats your browser cannot decode, an optional FastAPI upload service uses FFmpeg.

Why two players?

A browser can draw small colored rectangles efficiently and capture a camera without installing office software. But that preview is a custom grid, not a real office document. The native companion completes the original idea: it changes LibreOffice's CellBackColor properties through UNO, so video and live webcam footage actually pass through spreadsheet cells.

The downloadable ODS takes a third route: real styled cells, hidden frame data, and an embedded Basic player. The first frame appears immediately; moving through frames requires permitting the document's macro. There is no video or image laid over the grid.

Could another open-source grid be better?

Option License Best use here
Custom Canvas grid MIT application code Small dependency-free video/webcam preview; selected for this build
LibreOffice Calc MPL 2.0 + component licenses Actual native spreadsheet cells; selected for native playback and export
Glide Data Grid MIT A richer canvas-based interactive grid if editing and selection become central
Univer Apache 2.0 core A full browser spreadsheet editor; some important features are commercial Pro
Jspreadsheet CE MIT CE Spreadsheet editing; distinguish the community version from Pro

Those are project-documented licenses and capabilities. The suitability judgments are engineering recommendations, not a head-to-head speed benchmark. A complete office-suite server would add substantial machinery without being needed for local video sampling.

The real bottleneck is formatting

A 96 × 54 grid has 5,184 cells. At 12 requested frames per second, a full redraw could involve 62,208 cell color changes per second. Calc's data-array API writes values, not arbitrary per-cell background colors. The companion therefore skips unchanged cells and groups adjacent same-color pixels into ranges.

Controller notifications are suspended only while preparing an individual frame, then restored in a finally block. This uses LibreOffice's document controller API. Busy native connections keep only the newest pending frame, keeping the live feed from building up a long queue.

Requested FPS is not a native performance guarantee. The companion reports render time. Begin with 48 × 27 cells and monochrome or grayscale, then measure on your own computer.

Privacy and local connections

Browser conversion and webcam capture run on the device by default. Video is uploaded only when you configure the optional backend. Camera access requires a secure browser context and permission. Camera tracks stop when you switch sources or turn the camera off.

The companion listens on loopback, checks origins and Host headers, and requires a temporary bearer token. A hosted HTTPS page may be prevented from reaching a local HTTP service. The reliable route is opening the same web studio through the companion's local URL. UNO is bound to loopback; it is not an Internet-facing API.

Included, and intentionally bounded

The toolkit contains the whole web source, Python companion, optional FFmpeg API, ODS writer, tests, and research. Clips have at most 240 frames, preview grids at most 160 × 90 cells, and animated ODS exports at most 96 × 54. No audio is included. Converted data lives in tab memory until downloaded; there is no account system or cloud media storage.

This is a working prototype pipeline, not a public multi-user transcoding service. The included local FFmpeg backend has size, concurrency, and timeout limits; Internet exposure would additionally need authentication, user quotas and worker isolation.
